newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Brash aims to keep NZ inflation well inside target.
newsitem.headline: Brash aims to keep NZ inflation well inside target.

text.p: Reserve Bank of New Zealand Governor Don Brash said on Thursday he aimed to keep underlying inflation well inside the bank's new 0-3 percent inflation target.
The new coalition government last month widened the target from 0-2 percent.

Speaking to the Canterbury Employers' Chamber of Commerce, Brash said: "The Reserve Bank will be striving to keep inflation well inside the 0 to 3 percent range, and we best do that by trying to have inflation as close to the middle part of the range as possible."
He said the bank in no way had gone soft on fighting inflation and welcomed the wider band as probably meaning the target would be breached less often than in the past.

"That does not mean, of course, that we will always hit the target, any more than we always hit 0-2 percent. But it does mean that we will be constantly implementing monetary policy with the intention of having inflation as defined around the midddle part of the target.
"If we do this, the number of occasions on which we miss the target should be minimised. Indeed, given the wider target range, there should be fewer breaches than in the past."
Brash said he was concerned that some people believed that by broadening the target band, inflationary expectations could rise.
He said there was no evidence suggesting that monetary policy, by tolerating a little more inflation, could engineer higher sustainable growth in the long term.

"Not only is there no evidence that tolerating more inflation can engineer sustainably faster real growth, there is now overwhelming evidence that high inflation positively damages the way in which the economy works," he said.

He said that despite the new government's directive to the bank to target sustainable growth as well as price stability, the bank's maximum contribution would come by maintaining the focus on a stable general level of prices.
Brash said there was widespread debate on the right level of inflation to target, but there was no reason to be dogmatic.
He said the 0-3 percent target in his view was consistent with the intention of the legislation within which monetary policy was operated.
